name: Spider Plant
secondary_keywords: is spider plant safe for cats
question_title: How do you care for a spider plant in the UAE?
quick_answer: For spider plant care in the UAE, give the plant medium to bright indirect light, out of direct sun and AC airflow, and water thoroughly when the top of the soil is dry. A spider plant (Chlorophytum comosum) is non-toxic to cats and dogs. Brown leaf tips, a common problem, can come from salts or chemicals in water, dry soil or heavy feeding.

quick_facts.label: Light
quick_facts.value: Medium to bright indirect light. Tolerates deep shade. No direct sun: midday sun scorches the leaves.

quick_facts.label: Water
quick_facts.value: Let the soil dry slightly, then water thoroughly. Test the soil first; there is no fixed schedule. Water less in winter.

quick_facts.label: Temperature
quick_facts.value: Clemson Extension: 18–24 °C by day and 10–13 °C at night are ideal. NC State: keep it above about 7 °C.

quick_facts.label: Humidity
quick_facts.value: Average humidity suits it. Low humidity is one cause of brown tips. Humidity under AC varies from home to home.

quick_facts.label: Water quality
quick_facts.value: Chlorine, fluoride and salts in water can brown the leaf tips. Distilled water or rainwater helps (UW–Madison Extension).

quick_facts.label: Soil
quick_facts.value: General-purpose potting soil that drains well. The fleshy roots rot in soil that stays wet.

quick_facts.label: Feeding
quick_facts.value: Light. Too much fertiliser causes brown tips and fewer babies.

quick_facts.label: Babies (plantlets)
quick_facts.value: Form on long stems, mainly when days are short and nights are long and dark.

quick_facts.label: Size
quick_facts.value: About 30–45 cm tall. In a hanging basket the leaves and stems spread much wider.

quick_facts.label: Outdoors in UAE
quick_facts.value: Best kept indoors. Full sun burns it, and UAE summer heat is far above the range it prefers.

good_if: You have a cat or a dog: the ASPCA lists the spider plant as non-toxic to both.
You want a hanging or shelf plant with arching striped leaves.
Your room has medium light and no direct sun.
You like to grow new plants for free from the babies.
think_twice: Perfect leaf tips matter to you: brown tips are common and have many causes.
Your only free spot gets direct sun through a window or is on a sunny balcony.
You water often by habit: soil that stays wet leads to root rot.

care_sections.heading: How much light does a spider plant need?
paragraphs: A spider plant grows best in medium to bright indirect light. NC State Extension says it prefers medium light and can tolerate deep shade, and Clemson Extension says it grows best in bright indirect light.

Keep a spider plant out of direct sun. NC State Extension calls it intolerant of direct sunlight, and Clemson Extension warns that midday sun may scorch the leaves. In the UAE, keep it back from west- and south-facing glass, or put a sheer curtain on the window.

care_sections.heading: How often should you water a spider plant in the UAE?
paragraphs: Water a spider plant thoroughly when the top of the soil has dried slightly. UW–Madison Extension advises letting the soil dry slightly between thorough waterings, and Clemson Extension says to let it dry out briefly. There is no fixed schedule, because the right timing depends on your home.

Test the soil before you water: push a finger into the mix. If the top feels dry, water until water runs out of the drainage hole, then empty the saucer. If it feels damp, wait and test again later. A dry pot also feels much lighter than a freshly watered one.

What changes the timing for a spider plant: a small pot, a terracotta pot, a bright spot and warm months dry the soil faster; a large or plastic pot, a dim room, humid coastal air and winter dry it more slowly. NC State Extension advises watering less in winter. Check the soil, not the calendar.

A spider plant forgives the odd missed watering. UW–Madison Extension explains that its thick, fleshy roots store water, so the plant survives inconsistent watering. Soil that stays wet is the bigger risk: Clemson Extension and UW–Madison Extension both name overwatering and poorly drained soil as causes of root rot.

care_sections.heading: Can you use UAE tap water on a spider plant?
paragraphs: NC State Extension advises against tap water for a spider plant, because the chlorine and fluoride in it can cause leaf tip burn. Clemson Extension says water high in soluble salts burns the tips too.

UAE tap water is desalinated and then remineralised, and its mineral content varies by area and building. If the tips of a spider plant keep turning brown, UW–Madison Extension says distilled water or rainwater helps prevent tip browning. Clemson Extension says white to grey crusty deposits on the soil or pot rim are a sign of salt build-up: drench the pot with plenty of water to wash out the salts, let it drain and empty the saucer.

care_sections.heading: What temperature does a spider plant like, and how does it cope with AC?
paragraphs: A spider plant likes normal room temperatures. Clemson Extension gives 18–24 °C during the day and 10–13 °C at night as ideal, and UW–Madison Extension says it does well at cool to average temperatures but tolerates warmer conditions. Most AC homes and offices in the UAE are kept close to that daytime range.

Cold is a risk only in some places. NC State Extension says to keep a spider plant above about 7 °C. On the UAE coast, winter nights rarely come close to that indoors. Inland (Al Ain, desert areas, mountain areas) and in colder GCC cities, keep the plant away from cold windows and doors on winter nights; Clemson Extension also advises moving it away from windows to protect it from winter draughts.
Illinois Extension advises protecting houseplants from blasts of hot and cold air from heating and air-conditioning vents, so do not put a spider plant in the direct airflow of an AC vent.

care_sections.heading: Does a spider plant need humidity?
paragraphs: A spider plant does well in average humidity, according to UW–Madison Extension. Low humidity is one cause of brown leaf tips (Clemson Extension, UW–Madison Extension), but it is not the only one, so check the water and the soil first.

AC rooms in the UAE are not always dry: humidity under AC varies from home to home and between coastal and inland areas. To know the real humidity near a spider plant, use a simple hygrometer. If the air is dry, NC State Extension suggests a humidifier or a tray of pebbles and water under the pot.

care_sections.heading: What soil and pot does a spider plant need, and when should you repot?
paragraphs: A spider plant needs a general-purpose potting soil that drains well (Clemson Extension, UW–Madison Extension). Extra water must be able to leave the roots, because soil that stays wet leads to root rot. A pot with a drainage hole is the easiest way to let it out. If the plant sits in a decorative cover pot, lift it out to drain after watering, or empty any water that collects in the cover pot.

A spider plant grows thick, fleshy roots that fill a pot quickly. Clemson Extension advises dividing and repotting before the roots expand enough to crack the container, and says you can repot at any time of year. Do not rush into a much bigger pot: UW–Madison Extension notes that spider plants grow and produce babies best when slightly pot-bound. In the UAE, the cooler months are the easiest time to repot.
steps: Choose a pot a little wider than the old one, with a drainage hole, and fresh general-purpose potting soil.
Ease the spider plant out of the old pot. If the roots are tightly packed, you can divide the clump now.
Set the plant at the same depth as before and fill around the roots with fresh soil.
Water thoroughly until water drains out of the pot.
Clemson Extension advises waiting four to six months before feeding a newly potted plant.

care_sections.heading: Should you fertilise a spider plant?
paragraphs: Yes, feed a spider plant, but lightly and only while it is actively growing. Clemson Extension recommends a water-soluble or slow-release houseplant fertiliser used as the label says. UW–Madison Extension says feeding every three to four months is usually enough, or more often at half strength.

More fertiliser does not mean more spider plant babies. NC State Extension and UW–Madison Extension both say heavy feeding reduces the number of plantlets, and too much fertiliser burns the leaf tips (Clemson Extension).

care_sections.heading: How do you propagate a spider plant from its babies?
paragraphs: A spider plant is one of the easiest houseplants to propagate. It grows small plantlets, often called babies or spiderettes, on long stems, and UW–Madison Extension calls them extremely easy to root. Clemson Extension says you can start new plants from the plantlets at any time of year, and larger plants can also be divided when you repot.

Spider plant babies form mainly when days are short. NC State Extension says the mother plant needs short days and long, uninterrupted nights for at least three weeks; Clemson Extension notes that most offshoots appear as days shorten in autumn. In the UAE, that matches the autumn and winter months.
steps: Choose a baby that has started to grow small roots at its base.
Rest it on a small pot of moist potting soil next to the mother plant, still attached. Clemson Extension notes that plantlets root when they touch soil.
Once it has rooted into the soil, cut the stem that joins it to the mother plant.
Or cut off a baby that already has roots and pot it straight into moist potting soil (Clemson Extension, UW–Madison Extension).
Keep the new plant in bright indirect light and test the soil before each watering.

care_sections.heading: Where should you place a spider plant at home or in the office?
paragraphs: A spider plant looks best where its arching leaves and babies can hang down: a hanging pot, a high shelf or the edge of a desk. Clemson Extension says it grows quickly to about 60–75 cm wide and 60–90 cm long in a hanging basket.

Choose a spot with bright indirect light, out of direct sun and out of the airflow of AC vents. Because the ASPCA lists the spider plant as non-toxic to cats and dogs, it suits homes with pets, though a hanging pot also keeps the leaves away from a cat that likes to chew.

varieties.name: 'Vittatum'
varieties.look: Green leaves with a wide creamy-white stripe down the centre
varieties.care: Same care; UW–Madison Extension says it tends to grow more slowly than green types
varieties.best_for: The classic striped look; Clemson calls it the most common variegated cultivar

varieties.name: 'Variegatum'
varieties.look: Green leaves with white or cream edges
varieties.care: Same care; UW–Madison Extension says it tends to make fewer babies

first_week.intro: A move to a new home is a big change for a plant. A few bent or yellow leaves after delivery are a common reaction to the journey and a new spot.
steps: Put the plant in medium to bright indirect light, away from direct sun and out of the airflow of AC vents.
Test the soil. If the top feels dry, water thoroughly and empty the saucer; if it feels damp, wait.
Leave it in one spot so it can adjust.
Repot only if roots are pushing out of the pot. After repotting, Clemson Extension advises waiting four to six months before you feed it.

uae_year.care: Keep a spider plant indoors, out of direct sun through glass. Pots in warm, bright rooms dry out faster, so test the soil more often. Do not move it to a balcony: full sun burns it and outdoor heat is far above the range it prefers.
Days shorten, and a spider plant makes most of its babies now (Clemson Extension). Long, dark nights help, so a room where lights stay on late may give fewer babies. Root the babies as they appear.

NC State Extension advises watering a spider plant less in winter. Test the soil before each watering. Coastal homes stay warm enough. Inland (Al Ain, desert areas, mountain areas) and in colder GCC cities, keep the plant away from cold windows and doors at night.
Repot or divide a spider plant if roots fill the pot, before the summer heat. Feed lightly while it grows.

problems.question: Why are my spider plant's leaf tips turning brown?
problems.cause: Chemicals or salts in water, too much fertiliser, dry soil or low humidity
problems.answer: Brown tips are a common spider plant problem, and they have several causes. UW–Madison Extension lists low humidity, very dry soil, salt build-up and chemicals in water, especially fluoride and chlorine. Clemson Extension adds too much fertiliser and water high in soluble salts. Check the water and the soil first.
problems.signs: Dry brown tips, sometimes with a white crust on the soil or pot rim.
fix: Switch to distilled water or rainwater (UW–Madison Extension).
Drench the pot with plenty of water and let it drain, to wash out salts (Clemson Extension).
Feed less, and only while the plant is growing.
Water before the soil dries out completely.
If the air near the plant is dry, use a pebble tray or a humidifier (NC State Extension).
Trim the brown parts off with scissors if you do not like the look. Iowa State Extension notes that new browning appears if the cause is not fixed.

problems.question: Why are my spider plant leaves turning yellow and limp?
problems.cause: Usually too much water or poor drainage (root rot)
problems.answer: Yellow, limp spider plant leaves usually point to a watering problem. Clemson Extension says yellowing is most often a symptom of overwatering, and that root rot comes from soil that does not drain quickly or from excessive watering. Feel the soil: if it is wet, the roots may be rotting.
problems.signs: Soil that stays wet, water standing in the saucer or cover pot, a heavy pot.
fix: Stop watering and let the soil dry slightly.
Empty the saucer or cover pot, and check that the drainage hole is not blocked.
If the soil stays wet, take the plant out, cut out soft or rotten roots and repot in fresh, well-drained potting soil (Clemson Extension).
If the soil is bone dry instead, water thoroughly until water drains out.

problems.question: Why is my spider plant not producing babies?
problems.cause: Days too long or nights not dark, too much fertiliser, or a pot that is too big
problems.answer: A spider plant makes babies in response to short days and long, uninterrupted nights for at least three weeks (NC State Extension). Heavy feeding reduces plantlets (NC State Extension, UW–Madison Extension), and plants produce them best when slightly pot-bound (UW–Madison Extension).
problems.signs: Healthy leaves but no long stems or babies.
fix: Keep the plant in a room that gets dark at night, away from lamps that stay on late.
Feed less.
Do not move it to a much bigger pot.
Be patient: most babies appear as days shorten in autumn (Clemson Extension).

problems.question: Why does my spider plant have scorched patches?
problems.answer: Scorched patches on a spider plant are a sign of too much direct sun. NC State Extension calls the plant intolerant of direct sunlight, Clemson Extension warns that midday sun may scorch the leaves, and UW–Madison Extension says it can sunburn in full sun outdoors. In the UAE this often happens near west- or south-facing glass or on a balcony.
problems.signs: Pale or brown burnt areas on the side that faces the window.
fix: Move the plant to bright indirect light, or add a sheer curtain.
Trim badly damaged leaves at the base with clean scissors.

problems.question: What are the bumps or white cotton on my spider plant?
problems.symptom: Small bumps or white cotton on leaves
problems.answer: Small brown bumps or white cottony clusters on a spider plant are most likely scale insects or mealybugs, which UW–Madison Extension names as the main pests. Clemson Extension also lists whiteflies, spider mites and aphids.
problems.signs: Bumps or white fluff along the leaves and at the base, sticky residue, slow growth.
fix: Move the plant away from other plants until the pests are gone.
Wipe the pests off the leaves with a damp cloth.
For a heavier infestation, use a spray whose label allows indoor use on houseplants, and follow the label exactly.

problems.question: Why are thick roots pushing my spider plant out of its pot?
problems.symptom: Roots bulging out or a cracked pot
problems.cause: The fleshy roots have filled the pot
problems.answer: A spider plant grows thick, fleshy tuberous roots (Clemson Extension). When they fill the pot, they push the plant up and can crack the container. Clemson Extension advises dividing and repotting before that happens.
problems.signs: Roots on the soil surface or through the drainage hole, a pot that bulges, water that runs straight through.
fix: Take the plant out of the pot.
Divide the clump into pieces, each with leaves and roots, or move it to a pot a little wider.
Repot in fresh general-purpose potting soil and water thoroughly.

mistakes.mistake: Watering on a fixed weekly schedule
mistakes.instead: Water when the top of the soil has dried slightly. Test with a finger first.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the pot standing in water
mistakes.instead: Empty the saucer or cover pot after watering. Wet soil leads to root rot.

mistakes.mistake: Feeding often to get more babies
mistakes.instead: Feed lightly. Heavy feeding gives fewer babies and brown tips.

mistakes.mistake: Direct sun through a west- or south-facing window
mistakes.instead: Medium to bright indirect light, or a sheer curtain on the window.

mistakes.mistake: Moving it into a much bigger pot
mistakes.instead: Go up only a little. It makes babies best when slightly pot-bound.

mistakes.mistake: Putting it on a balcony for the summer
mistakes.instead: Keep it indoors. Full sun burns it.

myths.myth: A spider plant cleans the air in your home.
myths.fact: Not in a normal room. A 2019 review by Cummings and Waring found that a building would need 10 to 1,000 potted plants per square metre to match the air exchange it already has.
The opposite: heavy feeding reduces the number of plantlets (NC State Extension, UW–Madison Extension).

myths.myth: Brown tips mean the plant is dying.
myths.fact: Brown tips are common and have many causes, from water quality to dry soil (UW–Madison Extension). The rest of the plant can be healthy.

myths.myth: A spider plant is a type of spider lily.
myths.fact: They are different plants. The spider plant is Chlorophytum comosum, in the asparagus family (Asparagaceae); spider lilies belong to other genera, such as Hymenocallis.

pet_safety.summary: Yes, a spider plant is safe for cats and dogs: the ASPCA lists Chlorophytum comosum as non-toxic to both, and NC State Extension also lists it as non-toxic.
pet_safety.emergency: If your pet eats a large amount of any plant and vomits or seems unwell, call your vet and tell them the plant name.

faqs.q: Can a spider plant live in low light?
faqs.a: Yes. NC State Extension says a spider plant prefers medium light but can tolerate deep shade. Clemson Extension says it grows best in bright indirect light.

faqs.q: Does a spider plant clean the air?
faqs.a: A spider plant does not noticeably clean the air in a normal room. The studies that found plants removing chemicals were done in small sealed chambers. A 2019 review by Cummings and Waring concluded that a building would need 10 to 1,000 plants per square metre of floor to match normal air exchange. Buy a spider plant for its looks, not as an air filter.

faqs.q: Can a spider plant grow outside in the UAE?
faqs.a: A spider plant is best kept indoors in the UAE. UW–Madison Extension says that outdoors it needs bright light but can sunburn in full sun, and that in warm climates it is grown in partly shaded areas. UAE summer heat is far above the range Clemson Extension gives as ideal. A shaded outdoor spot is possible in the cooler months on the coast; bring it in before summer and before cold inland nights.

faqs.q: How big does a spider plant get?
faqs.a: A spider plant grows about 30–45 cm tall (NC State Extension, UW–Madison Extension). It spreads wider than it is tall: Clemson Extension says it reaches about 60–75 cm wide and 60–90 cm long in a hanging basket.

Yes. A spider plant grows small, white, star-shaped flowers on its long stems, and the babies form on the same stems (NC State Extension). Flowers usually appear after short days and long nights, but indoors they can appear at any time of year (UW–Madison Extension).

faqs.q: Why are the stripes on my spider plant fading?
faqs.a: Fading stripes are normal in some spider plant cultivars. NC State Extension says 'Hawaiian' shows variegation on new leaves that fades with age, and UW–Madison Extension says the narrow white line of 'White Stripe' is lost as the leaf ages.
